articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Education in the Space and Satellite Community' (Digest No.161)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: The author covers the International Space University (ISU) as a post-graduate course, and its relevance to a young professional's responsibilities and career development. ISU was founded by three young entrepreneurs in April 1987. ISU aims to bring together space experts from industry, academia and government, and to centre the interchange of enthusiastic international ideas. The author discusses the course content, its relevance, and future aims.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Satellite communications continuing education at York
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: The late 1980s saw the emergence of strong interest in systems employing VSATs-very small aperture terminals (sometimes called microterminals). These small dish systems offer a number of opportunities for communication; for example, one major asset is their 'bypass' feature, meaning that a PTT infrastructure may be totally avoided. This is attractive especially to large organisations with a number of dispersed sites, and to multi-national companies. Due to the lack of technically based courses on VSATs, the University of York mounted a short course in April 1990 entitled 'Small Terminal Satellite Communications: VSAT Systems, Technology and Opportunities'. The author discusses the aims of the course, the course content, how the course was marketed, the costing, and how successful the course was.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Professional training requirements in the UK space industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: Each year there are about 80 graduates directly entering the space industry as their first choice of career. At least 20% of these can be expected to want to take post-graduate degrees in a science or engineering discipline a few years later. In addition there is inwards migration of qualified but more mature engineers who will swell the ranks of the post-graduate degree students. Engineers from both sources require a continuous programme of specialist training to keep abreast of relevant technologies, funded by industry to a total value of Pounds 1 million. The author discusses the four elements of the training programme at Marconi Space: undergraduate professional training, internal training, specialist courses, and product support training.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The importance of technology in remote sensing and image processing training
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: The space community has such a variety of projects that a 'typical' set of skills might be impossible to define. It is clear that all the skills needed could not be taught in any single undergraduate degree course. Edinburgh University have tried to create a postgraduate course (a one year M.Sc.) which will give graduates with suitable first degrees the opportunity to complement their existing knowledge with skills they will find immediately useful in the space community. The first six months of the course consist of lecture, tutorials and practical work, leaving six months for a substantial dissertation project. The lectures form part of a modular scheme to allow this M.Sc. course to be well integrated with other M.Sc.s in Astronomical Technology and Information Technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: The author presents the factors involved in developing and implementing a training program for satellite operations staff. In particular, the author makes reference to the training for the Inmarsat second generation satellite system, which was spread over six months of 1990. The operations staff need sufficient expertise to be able to respond immediately to any emergencies and they must be able to demonstrate their proficiency in a safe manner, before they can be permitted access to the system itself. The author discusses the nature of satellite operations and how the training is linked to the operations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Satellite communication systems as part of an integrated communications course
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: Three years honours B.Eng. degree courses are still very popular with Electronic and Electrical Engineering students. Swansea University offer mainly option courses in the final year along with a major (student chosen) project. One of the courses is called 'Distributed Control and Integrated Communications'. As with other courses it is a 48 unit (lectures) courses, with 24 being on integrated communications. Satellite communication systems need to be met within this twenty-four unit course. The author outlines the satellite systems content of this course. This covers radio path propagation, space dynamics, disk antenna gain and satellite service prediction.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Training in satellite engineering provided by the University of Surrey
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: The University of Surrey has achieved a leading role in satellite engineering via its construction and launch of four low Earth orbit satellites (1981-1990) and its introduction of a unique MSc in satellite communication engineering in 1984. Together with an extensive research programme in satellite communications and space-craft engineering as well as a short course programme and schools activities, the University now covers the whole gambit of satellite education and training. This has led in 1990, to the foundation of a multi-disciplinary satellite engineering research centre at the University. The author describes the MSc course, the short courses and continuing education, research and the new satellite centre at the University.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Education in the space and satellite community . . . spreading the word
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: In order to target information with some degree of efficiency, education is typically performed at a number of levels. Thus education in space technology is aimed at the following target groups: engineers and scientists in industry (and elsewhere), students at universities and polytechnics, students at schools and colleges, and the general public. The author discusses education in each of these target groups. The author stresses the importance of introducing space education programs to children at school and briefly discusses the difficulties of educating the general public. The author suggests that to 'spread the word' and improve the prospects for UK space education, members of the public from primary school to parliament should be informed and inspired about space technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of signals from weather satellites in education
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: Receiving the signals from weather satellites and turning them into pictures is an excellent way of introducing students to satellite communications. It illustrates many of the problems and their solutions. The author describes the two types of weather satellite, geostationary and polar orbiting. The author then describes when and how weather satellite pictures can be received including a description of the equipment required.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sat. comms. talk for school VIth forms
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: In 1985 the author was asked to give a talk to a local scientific society and chose the topic 'Satellite Communications' because he was interested in it himself. Since then it has been repeated, with only small changes, to undergraduate and postgraduate audiences within King's College, as part of public relations for the Communications Research Group. The author believes talks of this kind could be very popular in schools and colleges because the audience mostly has an adequate basis of scientific knowledge and of relevant everyday experience from which to catch their interest as potential students and workers in the 'satellite' community. The author gives a plan of the talk and details the major contents of the talk.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Space engineering education at Kingston Polytechnic
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in the Space and Satellite Community
abstract: It is anticipated that the period 1990 to 2010 will see an expansion in space activities, both in the United Kingdom and Europe. It is to be expected that this will lead to an increase in demand for engineers and scientists with knowledge and expertise in space technology and associated fields, coupled with an increased student demand for degree courses with a space-related content. Since 1985 Kingston Polytechnic has been moving towards fulfilling this demand and has introduced space engineering as a component of its aerospace engineering degree course. The author gives a brief outline of the present form that space engineering education takes at Kingston, describes its success to date, and outlines some possible plans for the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
